doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

chapter: Swing, hot jazz and the bebop split
title: His rhythm guitar monograph and what swing is
summary: He describes his book on rhythm guitar and argues that swing cannot be forced, only allowed to happen.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well I’m writing a book, believe it or not, a monograph on rhythm guitar, the history of. Somebody asked me to do it and by the time I get finished with it I’ll have made a penny a page or something. Because it’s a labor of love. And in it I try to describe, first of all, to tackle those problems, the questions, the terms that nobody can really define. What is swing? You know, and I describe it, it’s more one of those qualities, it’s like if you ask somebody what is the feeling of well being? Well, nobody can really, it’s really very hard to define. You notice it first most I suppose by its absence. When things are wrong, when you feel sickly or ill, you know, but you don’t usually get up in the morning and say, “Gosh, I feel great today, I have a feeling of well being.” You know, the same thing here. Good playing with good time, articulating the time properly, and eventually getting into swinging, is something that you know, you don’t usually say, “Gee we’re playing with good time. Gosh, we’re really swinging.” It should just come naturally. And I usually tell the musicians, you know and I say to them, I often say to them, “Don’t swing, don’t cook, don’t sauté, don’t do anything, don’t braise, nothing.” I say, “Just play the song. Play the song with a good tone, the right changes, a nice beat, and if it’s gonna happen.” It’s like making love you know, you can’t bang the door down and seize the girl and throw her on the bed, “This is it.” You’ve got to have a little din din, you’ve got have a little drinky poo, you’ve got to look at the moon. You know what I mean, you’ve got to © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

have a little chance to get acquainted. It’s like that. And the same thing with music. Sometimes these jazz guys, you know they come loaded, like, “We’re gonna swing, we’re gonna cook tonight.” [scats] I mean where is there, what’s going to happen, it’s rather unnatural to me.
Yeah, and where is it going to go from there?

Natural is, you know [scats] just play. If it’s gonna get there, it’ll get there. If it isn’t, all the histrionics and all the effort and all the straining isn’t going to make it happen. And I’ve seen that happen so many times. Guys are straining. They’re going to tell their story. But it doesn’t work. And what that magic ingredient is, what that compatibility is that brings this out, is hard to say. And I mean I don’t think anybody’s ever gotten to a definition, and probably they shouldn’t.
